# 19 · How to decide whether another agent would help

## Start here

You can learn delegation without configuring subagents. Begin with one assistant and a tiny testing task. If “agent” is unfamiliar, read the [agents and workflows primer](../guide/07-agents-and-workflows.md): an agent uses a model and available tools to take steps toward a goal.

For an SDET, splitting work can help when separate parts need separate attention: one review checks requirements while another checks test evidence. It can hurt when every part depends on an unfinished result. Your first skill is deciding what can be separated, not launching as many workers as possible.

## The idea in plain language

**Delegation** means assigning a bounded piece of work to another worker. Here, a worker might be another assistant session, a native subagent, or a person. The **parent** is the coordinator responsible for integrating the results. These names describe responsibilities, not seniority or guaranteed ability.

A **dependency** exists when one task needs the result of another. Two tasks are **parallel** when they can proceed independently at the same time. Asking two agents to work simultaneously does not remove a dependency. Reviewing tests that have not been written yet requires either waiting or reviewing a different, clearly identified existing version.

A useful worker brief says what to examine, what evidence it may use, what result to return, and what it may change. A read-only requirement checker can return requirement IDs and omissions. It does not need permission to rewrite the application. Giving each worker only useful context can make its job clearer, but missing essential context can produce confident guesses.

Integration is real work. Someone must check whether the findings refer to the same version, resolve conflicts, and verify the combined result. Two confident answers based on the same mistaken source do not become independent confirmation. A second worker is worthwhile when its contribution exceeds that extra coordination effort.

For a five-line requirement, one assistant with a clear checklist may be enough. For separate components with independently testable behavior, division can help. Choose the smallest setup that produces useful evidence.

## A small example

Signal Desk is reviewing this invented search feature:

```text
R1: Search ignores letter case.
R2: An empty query displays a helpful message.
Existing tests: one query, "Invoice", against a record named "Invoice".
```

One worker can inspect which requirements the existing test covers. Another can list missing input information, such as what the helpful message should say. Both use the same supplied facts and can work independently. Writing a final test suite from their findings comes afterward.

The parent should not simply merge every suggestion. A demand to test payment processing would be outside these requirements unless additional scope is supplied. The useful return is a finding with its basis, not a long list of generic testing ideas.

## Try it with Codex or Claude Code

1. Open a conversation in either assistant. For project access, use the [assistant quickstart](../../docs/ASSISTANT-QUICKSTART.md); this prompt also works by itself.
2. Paste the prompt below. It deliberately asks for a role demonstration, not real subagent execution.

```text
Teach me delegation using this complete synthetic example:
R1: Search ignores letter case.
R2: An empty query displays a helpful message.
Existing test: query "Invoice" against a record named "Invoice".
Show two short worker briefs: a requirement-coverage checker and a
missing-information checker. Both are read-only and must use only these facts.
Then demonstrate their outputs, labeled "single-conversation role simulation".
As coordinator, explain one integration check and which next task must wait.
Do not spawn real agents, run commands, edit files, or write a full test suite.
Use plain language and no more than 300 words.
```

3. Inspect whether each brief has a distinct job. Check whether its output actually uses the supplied requirement or test.
4. Ask: “What would be lost if I did this with one assistant instead?” There may be no worthwhile benefit at this tiny scale.
5. If you later want actual workers, explicitly request them and inspect whether your assistant reports real separate worker execution. If the feature is unavailable, two manually managed sessions can illustrate separate contexts, but they do not demonstrate native orchestration.

## What you should see

The two roles should contribute different findings. A worker should report unknown wording as unknown, not invent an acceptance rule. The coordinator should distinguish tasks that can start immediately from tasks awaiting findings.

The answer must label its role-play honestly. Separate headings inside one answer are not evidence that multiple independent agents ran. Nor do two separate sessions automatically establish that their conclusions are correct.

## If it goes wrong

If both workers do the same job, narrow their briefs. If the assistant invents requirements, ask it to attach each finding to R1, R2, or an explicitly labeled question. If it produces a finished solution before you understand the roles, stop at the briefs. If real workers edit the same file, pause integration and establish one owner before continuing; do not assume the last writer's change includes the other's work.

## Optional practice

Ask your tutor for a small three-task job. Decide which task, if any, could start independently. Give your reason before requesting feedback; no diagram is required. The [original lesson 19](../lessons/19-delegation-design.md) retains the deeper design exercises. [Lab 13](../labs/13-coding-and-workers.md) later distinguishes scripted worker processes from actual assistant workers, so you can test the execution mechanism separately from the idea.
